title: Great Fire of London, Day 3: Why Did Samuel Pepys Bury His Cheese? A 1666 Diary
description:
On the evening of September 4, 1666, the third day of the Great Fire of London, Samuel Pepys and Sir William Penn dug the day's second pit in the yard and put their wine in it; then Pepys added "my Parmazan cheese" (my Parmesan cheese). This episode follows his own diary through the fire's first five days: on September 2 his maid wakes him, and he goes back to sleep; an officer at the Tower tells him the fire began in Pudding Lane; he proposes to the King and the Duke of York that houses be pulled down, but the Lord Mayor says people will not obey him; at noon he still hosts his guests, and at dusk, watching the fire from the far bank, he weeps; on September 3, in his nightgown, he rides with the cart carrying his money and silver away; on September 4, Sir William Batten buries his wine first and Pepys adds his office papers, and only that evening is the second pit dug; in the small hours of September 5 the fire reaches the end of his lane, but his house and office are saved; on September 6 he unloads his goods and writes "our fears over".

Limits: where the fire began is something he was told; "no one trying to put it out" covers only what he saw; the blasting that stopped the fire covers only the streets around him. The diary does not say why he buried the cheese, nor how big or costly it was, nor whether it was ever dug up; the video's "what couldn't be moved went to the earth" is our guess. Sources are listed below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the historical figures are cartoon characters, not likenesses.

lf101.text: If your street burned and you could hide only a few things, what would they be?

lf102.text: 1666, day three of the Great Fire of London. The fire nears one man's home; what he hides, you'd never guess.

lf103.text: Evening, September 4, in a London yard: Pepys and Sir William Penn are digging a pit.

lf104.text: It's already the yard's second pit that day.

lf105.text: They lay in wine, then he adds something of his own.

lf107.text: Fire has reached nearby streets, yet he crouches in the yard, digging.

lf108.text: But that's not the closest call. Around 2 a.m. the next day, his wife wakes him.

lf109.text: This file follows his own diary through the first five days of the fire.

lf110.text: With the fire so close, why would he bury a cheese in the ground?

lf201.text: The fire had begun two days earlier, before dawn. On September 2, his maid Jane saw fire in the City.

lf202.text: She woke Pepys. In his nightgown, he went to the window.

lf203.text: He looked; it seemed behind Mark Lane, still far from home.

lf204.text: And then? He really went back to bed and slept again.

lf205.text: Woken at night for a far-off fire, you'd likely go back to bed too, right?

lf206.text: By morning, he even thought the fire looked smaller.

lf207.text: But Jane brought news: she'd heard that over 300 houses had already burned.

lf208.text: A number she had heard. Pepys had to see for himself.

lf209.text: He climbed up high at the Tower. What would he see this time?

lf210.text: Houses at the bridge blazed; he feared for a friend's home on it.

lf211.text: A Tower officer told him it began in Pudding Lane, at the King's baker's house.

lf212.text: That was hearsay too; he didn't see the moment it started. I think that's worth making clear.

lf213.text: Was that friend's home still there?

lf214.text: He went by boat to look; people were loading goods onto barges.

lf215.text: Only on the water did he see the friend's house had already burned.

lf216.text: Some threw what they couldn't move in the river.

lf217.text: Some stayed till fire hit the door, then ran aboard.

lf219.text: He wrote that, at least in his sight, no one tried to put it out.

lf220.text: The wind drove it on into the City. Who could stop it?

lf301.text: Pepys had an idea. Instead of staying on the boat, he hurried to Whitehall.

lf302.text: He told the King and the Duke of York in person what he'd seen.

lf303.text: His idea: pull down houses ahead of the fire; only that might stop it.

lf304.text: The King had him tell the Lord Mayor: spare no houses.

lf305.text: The Duke of York offered soldiers if needed.

lf306.text: Reading this far, I thought there was hope.

lf307.text: But when he found the Lord Mayor, would anyone obey him?

lf308.text: The diary logs his complaint: no one obeys; the fire is too fast.

lf309.text: He said he'd been up all night and needed rest first.

lf310.text: Soldiers? He said he needed none, and walked away.

lf311.text: Picture it: the King's message delivered, and the messenger can only watch him walk off.

lf312.text: People were fleeing; even the churches were packed with goods left there.

lf313.text: Along the streets, bundles on backs, carts piled high.

lf314.text: Pepys made a point to note: tar on Thames Street, oil and wine in warehouses.

lf315.text: And his own wine at home?

lf316.text: When would the fire reach his own house?

lf401.text: Not by noon, at least. He went home and hosted the guests he'd invited.

lf402.text: The meal was still lavish, but all minds were on the fire.

lf403.text: Mrs. Batelier came asking after two relatives; Pepys noted their houses had burned.

lf404.text: You've likely had meals like that: good food, mind elsewhere.

lf405.text: Out after dinner, he saw goods taken in that morning moved even farther off.

lf406.text: That's strange: a place that felt safe in the morning was no longer safe by afternoon.

lf407.text: He got back on a boat. How far had the fire pushed now?

lf408.text: Above and below the bridge, it spread farther.

lf409.text: Boats full of goods crowded the river.

lf410.text: He also noticed many boats carried virginals, a small home keyboard.

lf411.text: A keyboard on a boat of rescued goods. When I first read that, I did a double take.

lf412.text: He edged closer into the wind; flying sparks drove him off. How far can sparks fly?

lf413.text: Houses several doors off caught fire in turn.

lf414.text: At dusk, from the far bank, the fire looked like one long arch.

lf415.text: He wrote that the sight made him weep.

lf416.text: You can imagine how vast that fire was.

lf417.text: At home, Tom, whose house had burned, came to stay with what little he saved.

lf418.text: News kept coming, so they had to start packing. But move things where first?

lf419.text: By moonlight, goods went to the garden first.

lf420.text: Tom helped put money and iron chests in the cellar; ledgers and papers elsewhere.

lf422.text: If he had to move again, what would go first?

lf501.text: The money went first. Before dawn on September 3, a neighbor sent him a cart.

lf502.text: In his nightgown, he rode guard over the money and silver.

lf503.text: Honestly, it's a bit of a funny picture; but I'd guess he wasn't laughing at all.

lf504.text: To a friend's house in Bethnal Green.

lf505.text: That house was already crammed with others' things.

lf507.text: He and his wife went home and kept moving things out.

lf508.text: Someone found him a barge. Whose things would ride on it too?

lf509.text: Chests, hauled over Tower Hill to the quay.

lf510.text: So crowded, no one could carry goods through a small gate.

lf511.text: A neighbor with a child put a few things on his boat too.

lf512.text: If you were fleeing too, would you share your boat?

lf514.text: He carried some himself, not just giving orders.

lf515.text: That night, the couple slept on a quilt in the office.

lf516.text: No pots or dishes; the two ate yesterday's leftovers.

lf517.text: Anyone who's moved knows: the last night, you eat whatever.

lf518.text: Cart, boat, garden, all used. What was left that couldn't be moved?

lf601.text: The wine. Early on September 4, what could move still went by boat.

lf602.text: By afternoon, fire was on Tower Street, nearing several houses.

lf603.text: Someone's plates and shovels lay scattered in the gutter.

lf604.text: Neighbor Batten couldn't move his wine; he found another way.

lf605.text: He dug a first pit in the yard and put his own wine in it.

lf606.text: Pepys seized the chance to add his office papers.

lf607.text: I'd never seen anyone archive files that way.

lf608.text: But that was Batten's pit. Remember the question on Thames Street? And his own wine at home?

lf609.text: That evening, he and Penn dug another pit for their own wine.

lf610.text: Once the wine was in, the cheese from the start went into the same pit, with a few other things.

lf611.text: That day's entry doesn't say how big or costly the cheese was, or if it was wrapped.

lf612.text: If you heard it was a precious treasure: at least these days' entries never say so.

lf613.text: The cheese was hidden for now, but could his office escape the fire?

lf614.text: In fact, earlier that afternoon, he had discussed this with Penn in the garden.

lf615.text: He proposed: bring dockyard workers from downriver to save it.

lf616.text: That night, Penn went to get the workers there by morning.

lf617.text: Pepys also wrote Sir William Coventry for leave to demolish.

lf618.text: But no reply came. Would anyone act first?

lf619.text: Supper was a shoulder of mutton with his wife and guests, without even a napkin.

lf620.text: Through the meal, he kept walking into the garden to look up at the fire-red sky.

lf621.text: At night he saw Tower Street houses blasted ahead of the fire.

lf622.text: Remember his pull-down plan at court? In the blasted area, the fire really stopped.

lf623.text: Reading this, I relaxed, but only halfway.

lf624.text: Tower Street held. But what about his own lane?

lf701.text: The fire soon found his lane. That 2 a.m. from the start was September 5.

lf702.text: His wife woke him: fire by the church at the lane's end.

lf703.text: This time, he didn't go back to bed.

lf704.text: He took his wife and money downriver by boat.

lf705.text: Looking back by moonlight, all London seemed to be burning. Would he go back?

lf706.text: He locked the money in a friend's house and had his wife and party guard it in turns.

lf707.text: Then he went back by boat himself.

lf708.text: With your money safe, would you go back to the fire? I probably wouldn't.

lf709.text: On the way back, at Deptford, he saw his goods still aboard, under guard.

lf710.text: He had assumed his house had already burned.

lf711.text: And? The house was still standing.

lf712.text: Nor had the office burned; he only believed it up close.

lf713.text: Fire stopped at the lane's church, singeing clock and porch.

lf714.text: The diary credits blasting and Penn's overnight workers for saving the street.

lf715.text: This part is a joy to read.

lf716.text: Climbing that church's tower, what London would he see?

lf718.text: Fires burned far off; he dared not stay long.

lf719.text: Embers burning their feet, they walked on.

lf720.text: Moorfields was packed with refugees guarding their goods.

lf721.text: He picked up a shard of glass bent by the heat.

lf722.text: Back at the office, he set men on night watch.

lf723.text: He lay down only at midnight, and slept better at last.

lf724.text: But once day broke, had the fire really stopped?

lf801.text: Not yet. Morning, September 6: a new fire at Bishopsgate.

lf802.text: Pepys and the men rushed over; it was soon out.

lf803.text: Along the river, he saw the houses and churches on the bank largely gone.

lf804.text: Remember the guarded goods at Deptford?

lf805.text: He landed them at Sir George Carteret's.

lf806.text: Afterward, he said nothing looked missing or damaged.

lf807.text: In that day's diary, he wrote:

lf809.text: Was the cheese in the yard ever dug up?

lf810.text: And the opening question: why did he bury it in the ground?

lf811.text: My guess: carts and boats had done their rounds; the wine and cheese they couldn't move went to the earth.

lf812.text: So, this file: cheese buried, closed. Why he buried it, and whether it was dug up, the diary never says: open.

lf813.text: If you were in that yard, what would you put in the pit? Tell me in the comments.

lf814.text: This channel only covers what the records show. Subscribe to open more files with us.
